title: The Case Against Complaining
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. argues that teachers should take their own habit of complaining seriously. He opens with a married pair of veteran teachers whose relentless problem-pointing seemed to mark an unhappy, stalled professional and personal life. He then tests the usual defenses of complaining (it is therapeutic, venting is healthy, it builds camaraderie) and finds them to be unproven articles of faith. His own case against it rests on three costs: wasted time, an inner distortion that breeds both powerlessness and pride, and, at the far end, complaint hardening into identity, illustrated through C. S. Lewis's The Great Divorce. He closes by asking readers only to question their justifications and to rejoice that complaining is one area of teaching life every teacher controls.
points: Distinguishes solutions-oriented discussion of problems from non-solutions-oriented complaint, so the target is the habit of grumbling, not honest problem-solving.
Shows that the common defenses of complaining (therapy, venting, camaraderie) are rationalizations that collapse under simple questions about evidence.
Argues complaining makes teachers feel both powerless and prideful, a warping of the heart that undermines their best work.
Uses Lewis's grumbler-versus-grumble image to warn that habitual complaint can become a person's identity.
Ends on agency: teachers cannot control many things but can choose whether to keep complaining.
quotes: The trouble, though, is that these cases for complaining are often unwarranted statements of faith. They don’t stand up well to simple, prodding questions, such as:

Since complaining isn’t solutions-oriented, a complaining session doesn’t make anything of value: there’s no product to help us do better work, no path forward through the thing that’s frustrating us. So, at best, complaining wastes the time it takes to complain.
What I’m saying is that there’s a warping of the heart that happens when we complain, and from the warped heart we can’t do our best work.

I think it’s possible for us, when we habituate complaint and place in our innermost circles those who will complain along with us, to have complaining become a part of us, a component of our identities.
If this post only makes you more of a moralist, more certain in your own goodness, then it’s a failed piece of writing.
There are so many things we can’t control, but every teacher in the world can choose whether or not to persist in complaining.
